title: Did the grader run twice? The trigger-flip share of run-to-run disagreement on HAL's tau-bench airline cells
claim: On tau-bench airline cells whose scaffold ends conversations unsolicited, most of the run-to-run disagreement a leaderboard would report is the grader not running in one of the two runs, not the agent solving the task in one and failing in the other.
trick: Line up the same model's two runs task by task and ask, for every task whose score differs, whether the score differed because the agent did something different or because the grader only ran once; if the second reason dominates, the 'run-to-run noise' of that cell is the measuring instrument switching itself off at random.
why_now: 2611.04399 (arXiv 2026-11-03) released the recipe and code (github.com/YangzeLiu/eval-instrument-disclosure) that mark which archived HAL episodes were graded ('An episode counts as graded when its record holds such an injected copy of the gold actions anywhere, or when its recorded reward is positive') and showed the ungraded half can be re-graded offline through the pinned commit with no model call; HAL's archives hold 'one or two runs of about 41 records each' per cell, so the paired second run already exists for part of the grid at $0. The paper treats the graded fraction as a level shift ('On this leaderboard the difference between the two scaffolds was a difference in whether the grader ran') and never asks whether the same tasks go ungraded twice; HAL's own reliability protocol attributes temperature-0 run-to-run variance to the serving stack (2602.16666 sec. 4, quoted on CL-W44-07). Nobody has split a leaderboard's replicate disagreement into trigger flips and outcome flips.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 2 days): decrypt the TAU-bench Airline archives with own code in the scratchpad (never the repository's scripts), list the (model, scaffold) cells with two runs and their run dates and recorded temperature or sampling settings from the run metadata, open one record's layout to confirm the action list, model outputs and ending events are present; re-implement the grader-action alignment and check it reproduces the paper's graded fractions (Generalist 51%, Tool-Calling 98%) on the pooled set. Step 1 ($0, 3 days): for every two-run cell compute $D_{\mathrm{pub}}$, $\tau$, $J$ and, after offline re-grading through the pinned tau-bench commit with the simulator stubbed (the paper's procedure; validation target: the recorded reward reproduced on graded records), $D_{\mathrm{all}}$; report Generalist and Tool-Calling cells separately, read-only and write-required tasks separately (the stub passes an untouched database on read-only gold), with a task-level bootstrap interval on $\tau$ and on $D_{\mathrm{pub}} / D_{\mathrm{all}}$ pooled over Generalist cells. Step 2 (only if step 0 finds fewer than three Generalist two-run cells; about $150, 0 GPU-h, 3 days): run HAL's released Generalist scaffold once more on the 41 airline tasks for three models that have one archived run (deepseek-v3, gpt-4.1, gemini-2.0-flash or whichever are still served), at the archive's recorded settings, through the same pinned tau-bench commit, and repeat step 1 on the new pairs.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Pooled over the Generalist two-run cells, the ungraded sets are stable ($J \geq 0.75$) and trigger flips are a minority of disagreements ($\tau \leq 0.2$ with the bootstrap upper bound under 0.35), so that $D_{\mathrm{pub}} / D_{\mathrm{all}} \leq 1.1$: whether the grader runs is then a property of the task under that scaffold, the paper's level-shift reading stands, HAL's replicate disagreement on these cells is agent and serving behaviour as HAL assumes, and the fix is the paper's reporting column ('accuracy 0.30, graded 51%') and nothing more. Also dead if step 0 finds the ungraded episodes carry a terminating event the paper's rule missed (then the quantity $G$ is not the one defined here).

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5: on Generalist cells the ungraded set moves between runs ($J$ between 0.3 and 0.6), trigger flips are at least 40% of the stored-reward disagreements ($\tau \geq 0.4$) and the published disagreement is at least 1.3 times the all-graded disagreement; on Tool-Calling cells $\tau$ is near 0 (graded 98%) and $D_{\mathrm{pub}} \approx D_{\mathrm{all}}$, so the two scaffolds' 'reliability' differs mostly in how often the instrument fires.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: 2611.04399 reads the ungraded half as a systematic scaffold term ('the difference between the two scaffolds was a difference in whether the grader ran'; 'Grading those episodes offline closes the Generalist's pooled deficit') and has no replicate; HAL attributes temperature-0 run-to-run variance to 'non-sampling sources of stochasticity [...] floating-point non-associativity, batch-size variation' (2602.16666 sec. 4); tau-bench defines pass^k as the consistency of the agent over $k$ runs (2406.12045), not of the grader; 2609.37315 holds that 'a defect beneath a score is present on every rerun', which predicts $J$ near 1.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If trigger flips dominate, a replicate rule on these cells measures the trigger, pass^k on scaffolds that close unsolicited is deflated by the trigger's reliability rather than the agent's (one ungraded run zeroes a task's pass^k), the paper's 'bias' is the mean of a noisy indicator and its per-model directions are weaker than stated, and the remedy is a grading rule that fires on agent exit (or a resume step), not a column. If the ungraded set is stable, the graded fraction is a deterministic scaffold-by-task property, the replicate disagreement HAL reports is clean of the instrument, and the reporting column is the whole fix — a footnote the owners can cite.

Requires step 2 for at least five cells and one pass^k recomputation. Judgment p 0.3.

Requires CL-W44-07's probe to run beside this and one more benchmark with a termination-gated grader. Judgment p 0.1.

title: Ask the user, not the database: resuming the simulated user on the Generalist episodes the offline re-grade passed
statement: Take every ungraded HAL Generalist episode on tau-bench airline (about half of the Generalist records; they 'end on a message to the user, at a median of nine actions'), rebuild the conversation as the pinned tau-bench commit's user simulator saw it, append the agent's unsolicited closing message, and sample the user's reply with the pinned user model and settings; record whether the user emits the stop token (accepts the ending) or continues, and classify a continuation as a pending request, an unanswered question or a pleasantry by the user's own text. Cross the acceptance with the paper's offline re-grade $\tilde r_i$ to get, for the ungraded episodes the re-grade passes, the acceptance rate $A = \Pr[\text{STOP} \mid \tilde r_i = 1,\ G_i = 0]$ separately on read-only gold (where the stub passes an untouched database) and on write-required gold (the paper's 23 episodes with the required write), with a per-task bootstrap. Zero agent runs; the only model calls are the user simulator's.
claim: An offline re-grade that stubs the simulated user pays the agent for hanging up: on tau-bench airline, the user accepts under half of the read-only episodes the stubbed re-grade passes, so the audited 13-point gap closes to a tie only under a rule the benchmark's own second party rejects.
trick: The paper scored the ungraded conversations by checking the database with the customer removed from the room; put the customer back, show them the agent's goodbye, and count how often they say 'that's all, thanks' rather than 'wait, I still need...'.
why_now: 2611.04399 (2026-11-03) states the gap itself: 'The HAL re-grades use the tau-bench commit HAL's setup pins with the user simulator stubbed, so they evaluate the database and output criteria only' and 'Most of the pooled gain comes from tasks whose gold only reads the database, which the benchmark's rule passes whenever the episode leaves the database as it was'; it asks the owners whether an unsolicited closing is an ending and 'As of 3 November 2026 the tau-bench issue and the tau2-bench issue have no maintainer reply'. HAL has already posted correction notes on the paper's disclosures, so the stubbed number is becoming the record. The user simulator that decides the ending is the one piece of the benchmark the audit left out, and it is public at the pinned commit.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 2 days): decrypt the TAU-bench Airline archives with own code, open one Generalist record's layout and check whether the user simulator's reply to the closing message is already stored (the Generalist 'sends one closing message to the user and exits'; if the environment step that delivered the message also recorded a user reply, part of the arm is free); read the pinned tau-bench commit for the user simulator's model, system prompt, scenario injection and temperature; reproduce the paper's graded/ungraded partition and offline re-grade on the ungraded set. Step 1 (about $40 of user-simulator calls at the pinned model, 0 GPU-h, 3 days): for each ungraded Generalist episode (about 250 to 370 across nine models and one or two runs), construct the user-side transcript and sample the reply to the closing message $k = 5$ times if the pinned temperature is above 0 (once if it is 0); label STOP versus continuation; label continuations by rule (a pending scenario request not yet addressed; a question about information the agent never gave; a pleasantry) with two independent labelers and Cohen's $\kappa$ reported. Compute $A$ on read-only and write-required gold, the acceptance rate on ungraded episodes the re-grade fails (a control: the user should rarely accept those), and the corrected Generalist score under 'resume then grade': an ungraded episode counts as passed only if the user accepts and the offline rule passes. Step 2 (optional, about $200, 4 days): for the continuations that carry a pending request, resume the agent itself for at most ten more steps under HAL's released Generalist scaffold and grade by the protocol, to see how many of the 'solved tasks recorded as failures' finish when the conversation is allowed to end properly.
killing_experiment.kills_if: The simulated user emits the stop token for at least 80% of the ungraded episodes the stubbed re-grade passes, on read-only and write-required gold alike (bootstrap lower bound above 0.7), and accepts under 30% of the episodes the re-grade fails: the stub was harmless, the paper's corrected scores are the benchmark's own verdict, the tie headline stands, and the owners' silence is the only thing left to resolve. Also dead at step 0 if the pinned user simulator cannot be re-instantiated on a stored transcript (scenario state not recoverable from the record).

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5: on read-only gold the user accepts under half of the re-grade's passes (the scenario still holds a request the agent never reached in nine actions), on write-required gold over 70%; the resume-then-grade Generalist score lands between the published 0.30 and the paper's 0.43, closer to 0.36, so the 13-point gap narrows but does not close; the re-grade's fails are accepted under 20% of the time (the control holds).
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: 2611.04399: 'These are solved tasks recorded as failures' (write-required) and the pooled 0.30 to 0.43 as the corrected score, with the stub acknowledged as evaluating 'the database and output criteria only'; HAL's correction notes adopt the paper's reading; tau-bench's protocol (2406.12045) holds that the episode ends when the user emits the stop token, which implicitly makes the user the arbiter of completion; 2507.02825 (ABC) notes 'TAU-bench counts empty responses as successful', i.e. the rule is lenient in the other direction.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If the user accepts under half of the read-only passes, offline re-grades of multi-party benchmarks are not scores until the second party is resumed — a methodological rule for every audit that replays logs through a grader (Rollout Cards, ABA-style recomputation, HAL's own corrections), and the right repair for a termination-gated grader is resume-then-grade, not grade-anyway. If the user accepts nearly all, the stub is validated as a cheap stand-in and the benchmark owners' ending rule, not the auditor, is what penalised the Generalist — a result the owners' open issue can close with.

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2611.04399 sec. 8 (the stub sentence) and sec. 3.5 (no maintainer reply); HAL's correction notes (dated 2026-10-05) that now carry the stubbed re-grade; 2605.08545's position that log analysis must track execution, with tau-bench airline as its example; tau-bench 2406.12045's stop-token ending rule. Who pays: HAL (which number goes in the note), the tau-bench and tau2-bench owners (whether to grade on agent exit), auditors who re-grade from logs, and groups building user simulators (the simulator's acceptance decision is shown to be a grading decision).

impact_ceiling.floor: A note giving $A$ by gold type and the resume-then-grade Generalist score, cited by HAL's correction notes and the paper's v2. Requires step 1. Judgment p 0.55.

Requires steps 1-2. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The user simulator recognised as part of the instrument on tau-family benchmarks: acceptance behaviour measured across simulator models and temperatures as a grading-rate curve, changing how tau2-bench and HAL define an ending. Requires two more simulator models and tau2-bench's airline domain. Judgment p 0.1.

It is not a new user simulator, not a verdict on the paper's cost or provenance findings, not a replicate study (the sibling candidate), and not an argument about what the owners should have intended.

The agent is not resampled in step 1, so $A$ is a property of the user simulator's acceptance rule given the transcript — a property of the benchmark's protocol, which is the point: whether the stubbed re-grade equals the protocol's own verdict. The paper's offline re-grade $\tilde r_i$ is deterministic given the record. Step 2 resamples the agent and is reported separately with its temperature. Judge and verifier are distinct here: the database rule is the verifier, the user's STOP is the protocol's completion event, and no LLM judge is used.

title: Same defect, two repairs: tightening the instruction and loosening the test lift different agents on the Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks both Z.ai and the maintainers fixed
statement: For the Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks whose instruction and tests disagreed and that were repaired twice — by Z.ai's Terminal-Bench 2.0 Verified, which 'edits the instruction to state what the test checks', and by Terminal-Bench 2.1, which 'more often edits the test to accept any correct solution' (the 11 shared tasks minus the four on which 2.1 adopted Verified's fix) — build three arms on the 2.1 image: the 2.0 instruction with the 2.0 tests (broken baseline), the Verified instruction with the 2.0 tests (tighten), and the 2.0 instruction with the 2.1 tests (loosen), confirmed by file diff to differ in that one field. Run four models spanning the board's ability bands under one pinned harness (Terminus-2) with five trials per cell and read, per task and arm, the gain over baseline for each model, $g_a^{\mathrm{arm}}(t) = \hat p_{a,t}^{\mathrm{arm}} - \hat p_{a,t}^{\mathrm{base}}$, the between-repair disagreement $\Delta_a(t) = g_a^{\mathrm{tighten}}(t) - g_a^{\mathrm{loosen}}(t)$ against the five-trial replicate interval, and the sign of the top-band minus mid-band gain under each arm.
claim: Two maintainers' repairs of the same broken benchmark task lift different agents by more than the replicate floor: loosening the test lifts the agents already producing correct solutions the old test rejected, tightening the instruction lifts the agents who could nearly solve it, so 'repaired' is a maintainer's convention that reorders the middle of the board.
trick: When a task's instructions and its tests disagree there are two honest fixes — tell the agent what the test wants, or make the test accept what the agent honestly did — and the two fixes reward different agents; run both fixes on the same tasks and see whether 'the repaired version' is one thing or two.
why_now: Two independent public repairs of the same 11 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks now exist with their files: Z.ai's Terminal-Bench 2.0 Verified (Hugging Face dataset card; 11 instruction fixes plus environment fixes on all 89 images) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (released 2026-05-08; github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-2 PR #53), and 2611.08417 (arXiv 2026-11-05) names the convention split in its own words: 'when an instruction and its test disagree, Verified edits the instruction to state what the test checks, whereas Terminal-Bench 2.1 more often edits the test to accept any correct solution; stating the grader's expectation tells the agent part of the solution, while relaxing the grader leaves the task as hard as its contributor intended' and 'It adopts Verified's repair on four tasks'. The paper measures agreement between auditors on the flag ($\kappa = 0.80$) and never between repairers on the outcome; its load-bearing assumption is that a repair restores a unique intended task. The pipeline's CL-W44-11 treats 'content-repaired' as one set; this says whether it is.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 2 days): from the Verified dataset card, the TB 2.0 repository at the 2.0 tag and PR #53, list the 11 shared tasks, mark the four where 2.1 adopted Verified's fix, and for the remaining tasks diff instruction.md, the test files, the oracle solution and task.toml between 2.0, Verified and 2.1; keep only tasks where Verified changed the instruction and not the tests and 2.1 changed the tests and not the instruction (expected five to seven); record Table 7's pooled 2.0 and 2.1 pass rates for them. Build the three arms on the 2.1 image (environment fixes held common so that Verified's harness-specific image changes, e.g. procps and the Read-tool note, do not enter). Step 1 (about $600 of API spend, 0 GPU-h, 5 days; or about 80 GPU-h if the open models are served locally): four models at the paper's pinned settings under Terminus-2 — Qwen 3.5 27B and Gemma 4 31B (low to middle band on 2.0 per the paper's Table 5-6 entries), GLM 5.1 (upper middle) and GPT 5.4 mini (upper) — five trials per (task, arm, model), about 7 x 3 x 4 x 5 = 420 trials, per-trial failure reason logged (timeout, test failure, agent error), infrastructure-failed trials replaced and counted. title: Common random numbers at temperature 0: the environment's draws versus the serving stack as the source of outcome flips on a tool-stochastic agent benchmark
statement: On AgentCE-Bench (2604.06111; a grid-scheduling task whose tool calls are 'resolved via static JSON files', so the only exogenous randomness is the tool-failure channel that card 2611.05650 found drawn from a process-global random stream no snapshot records), take 24 boundary states (6 domains x hidden slots {5, 21} x anchors {1/3, 2/3} on the 5 x 7 grid, the card paper's own cells) reached by one open-weight model's live run at temperature 0 with the failure channel off, rebuild each state by re-executing the recorded prefix (the paper's prefix-rebuilt reference, 24/24 agreement), and continue the same model $k = 5$ times from the anchor at tool-failure rate $r \in \{0.05, 0.20\}$ under four cells that switch the two noise channels on and off: serving bitwise (single-request, fixed seed, verified by 20 re-sends before the run) or batched (the same vLLM server under 16 concurrent forks), and tool-failure draws coupled (every fork restored to the same stream position, common random numbers) or independent (one seed per fork). Readouts per state and cell: the share of fork pairs whose per-call action sequence differs, the first-divergence call index, the outcome flip count $F = \min(\sum_{j} Y_j,\, k - \sum_{j} Y_j)$ with $Y_j \in \{0,1\}$ the grader's verdict on fork $j$, and the within-state outcome variance $\hat p (1 - \hat p)$ with $\hat p = k^{-1} \sum_j Y_j$; the bitwise-and-coupled cell is the certificate (zero divergence by construction, as the paper's 0/24), the bitwise-and-independent cell isolates the environment's draw channel $E$, the batched-and-coupled cell isolates the serving channel $S$, and the batched-and-independent cell is the benchmark as run. A hosted frontier lane repeats the coupled and independent cells at temperature 0 through REST (serving cannot be made bitwise there, so its coupled cell is the live-vs-live serving floor the card paper calls the distributional control).
claim: On a tool-using agent benchmark run at temperature 0 with one in five tool calls failing at random, holding the environment's failure draws fixed across replicates removes more of the run-to-run outcome flips than making the serving path bitwise does: the environment's draw channel, not the serving stack, is the larger source of temperature-0 outcome variance.
trick: Give every replicate the same dice for the environment's tool failures (the simulation field's common random numbers) and, separately, the same arithmetic for the model's serving, then count which of the two, when switched off, stops the outcomes from flipping.
why_now: Card 2611.05650 (2026-11, NeurIPS 2026 IAB workshop) is the first measurement that the exogenous randomness an agent environment consumes lives outside every snapshot field ('no snapshot field records the stream's position') and that fixing it couples replicates exactly ('Capturing it yields exact replay for this probe by coupling the exogenous randomness across clones (common random numbers [15]; record-and-replay [22])'), while leaving the model-driven case open: 'whether realization-level infidelity moves model-driven behavior is unmeasured' (sec. 3.2). Its B.7 result (a controlled serving path 34/34 calls bitwise, a hosted path 0 of 4) and its sentence 'Temperature-zero decoding is not reproducible across runs in general [1], and greedy decoding diverges across batch sizes and hardware under 16-bit precision [33], so a hosted pathwise certificate must be measured on the deployed configuration' give the second switch. With both channels switchable on one lightweight public testbed (AgentCE-Bench, 2026-04-07, static JSON tools), the share CL-W44-07 asserts can be measured by subtraction rather than inferred from first-divergence turns, and the paper's own design needs no snapshot layer because its prefix-rebuilt reference reproduces the live state.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (1 day, $0): clone AgentCE-Bench at revision 22ae16b7, locate the tool-dispatch layer's failure draw and the start-up seeding the paper describes (App. B.2), add a harness-side capture and restore of the stream state at the anchor, and verify the certificate cell: one open-weight model (gpt-oss-20b or Qwen3-30B-A3B under vLLM, temperature 0, single-request serving, fixed seed) continued twice from each of 24 prefix-rebuilt anchors with coupled draws must agree bitwise in action sequence on 24/24 states at both rates; 20 byte-identical re-sends of one request must return identical completions. If the certificate cell is not 24/24 the serving arm is not bitwise and the run stops until it is. Step 1 (3 days, about 12 GPU-hours): the 2 rates x 3 remaining cells x 24 states x 5 forks = 720 continuations (at most 10 attempts per slot, the paper's cap), with the per-call success/failure sequence, the action sequence, the grader verdict and the first-divergence index logged per fork. Step 2 (2 days, about $250): the hosted lane, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview through REST at temperature 0 (the model C-W44-07 uses, same launch window), coupled and independent cells, 2 rates x 2 cells x 24 states x 5 forks = 480 continuations. Analysis: per rate, the state-level outcome-flip shares $\bar F_E$, $\bar F_S$, $\bar F_B$ (mean of $F / \lfloor k/2 \rfloor$ over the 24 states) with 10,000-resample state bootstraps, the action-divergence shares likewise, and the serving share $\sigma = \bar F_S / (\bar F_S + \bar F_E)$ reported with its interval; the batched-and-independent cell checks that the two channels roughly add ($\bar F_B$ against $\bar F_S + \bar F_E - \bar F_S \bar F_E$) and the hosted lane's independent-minus-coupled difference is its $E$ estimate against the coupled cell as the serving floor.
killing_experiment.kills_if: At both tool-failure rates the serving share $\sigma \geq 2/3$ with the bootstrap lower bound above 0.5 on the local model, and on the hosted lane the independent-minus-coupled flip difference is inside the coupled cell's own bootstrap band: the environment's draws move action sequences but not outcomes (the card paper's 0/24 grader divergence carries over to a model-driven policy), the serving stack is the majority source of temperature-0 outcome variance even where one call in five fails, CL-W44-07 loses this testbed and keeps only the second-sampling-party benchmarks, HAL's attribution sentence stands for tool-stochastic single-agent environments, and the L4 same-snapshot probes may ignore stream capture for outcome estimands and must replicate against the serving floor instead. A second, protocol kill: if the certificate cell is below 24/24 on either rate after step 0 the serving arm is not bitwise and nothing downstream is reported.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5 at $r = 0.20$: the environment's draw channel flips outcomes in more states than the serving channel does ($\bar F_E > \bar F_S$, $\sigma < 0.5$), because an open-weight model at temperature 0 that meets a failed call retries, re-plans or stops, and over 7 to 8 calls per continuation (the paper's mean live lengths 7.04 and 8.13) at least one failure is realised in most forks; at $r = 0.05$ the two channels are of the same order ($\sigma \in [0.4, 0.7]$). Action-sequence divergence is near-total in every non-certificate cell (above 20 of 24 states), so the action-level readout does not separate the channels and only the outcome-level one does. On the hosted lane the coupled cell already flips outcomes in 5 to 10 of 24 states (the serving floor), and the independent cell adds 3 to 8 more at $r = 0.20$.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: Benchmark owners: HAL's protocol sentence (CL-W44-07's current_belief, as recorded there from 2602.16666 sec. 4): 'We set the temperature to zero so that any observed variance is attributable to non-sampling sources of stochasticity [17] (e.g., floating-point non-associativity, batch-size variation from concurrent server load, non-deterministic kernel scheduling...)', i.e. temperature-0 spread is the serving stack. The card paper, for its scripted policy: 'final-grader divergence under the oracle retry policy was 0/24 in every condition: an outcome-only metric would have hidden the problem' (sec. 3.2), i.e. the draw channel moves realisations, not outcomes, and whether a model is different 'is unmeasured'.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If $\sigma < 0.5$ at $r = 0.20$: a temperature-0 replicate rule on the serving side (bitwise or batch-invariant serving, which systems papers now sell as the fix) removes less than half of the outcome spread on any benchmark with a stochastic tool layer, and benchmark owners must seed or record the environment's draws per replicate and report the two shares; CL-W44-07 gains its first measured cell where both channels are switchable. If $\sigma \geq 2/3$ at both rates: tool-failure realisations are absorbed by the policy before the grader, the serving stack is the thing to fix, and the attribution standard's stream capture is a requirement for pathwise estimands only, not for outcome estimands, which simplifies every same-snapshot design under CL-W44-06.

Who pays: benchmark owners writing replicate rules (HAL, tau-bench, Terminal-Bench), training teams validating on AgentCE-Bench-style lightweight environments, and anyone running the card paper's eight-arm design or the L4 same-snapshot probes, who need to know whether to capture the stream.

Requires steps 0 and 1. Judgment p 0.55.

Requires steps 0 to 2 and the ordering holding on both. Judgment p 0.25.

Requires a second environment with a seedable stochastic tool layer (tau-bench's flaky-tool variant or a seeded user simulator) and about $1,500 more. Judgment p 0.1.

Narasimhan (tau-family): direct, a seeded tool-failure layer is the tau-bench-style environment's stochastic part. Systems route: moderate, bitwise versus batched serving is the arm and batch-invariant serving is the product being sold. It is not the card paper's eight-arm history-manipulation design, not a snapshot or checkpoint system, not a batch-invariant serving method, and not a claim about any history edit: the history is unedited in every cell.

title: Whose words are the unsupported entries? Widening the provenance gate's source set to the agent's own earlier turns, and counting the hedges compaction dropped
statement: Take the entries a provenance gate calls unsupported (Source-Judged Compaction's judge: no source in the environment outputs or the prior summary) on three corpora — the card paper's released handoff-audit run records (Qwen3-8B, gpt-oss-20b; histories with reasoning, summaries, rule and AI-confirmed labels; MIT / CC BY 4.0, $0), Compact-Bench's public paired full-history / summary continuations (2610.31710; 14 summarizers), and 50 AppWorld train+dev tasks run once in the public SJC harness with its Prompting baseline and its own judge — and match each such entry against a widening source set: $\mathcal{S}_0$ = environment outputs and prior summary (the gate's own set, so every entry is unmatched by definition), $\mathcal{S}_1 = \mathcal{S}_0 \cup$ the agent's earlier visible assistant turns, $\mathcal{S}_2 = \mathcal{S}_1 \cup$ system prompt and tool descriptions, $\mathcal{S}_3 = \mathcal{S}_2 \cup$ the agent's recorded reasoning (open-weight corpora only, with a flag for whether that reasoning was in the writer's input at compaction, which the card paper shows it is not for Qwen3). The matcher is the typed-value and content-word matcher of C-W44-11 with a shuffled-history placebo for its chance-match rate; the readouts are the unmatched share at each level, $u_\ell = |\{e \in E_0 : e \text{ has no match in } \mathcal{S}_\ell\}| / |E_0|$ with $E_0$ the gate's unsupported set, and, for entries matched in $\mathcal{S}_1$ or $\mathcal{S}_3$, the de-hedged share $h$: the earliest antecedent carries a hedge marker (might, may, probably, likely, I think, should check, TODO, not sure) and the summary entry carries none.
claim: Most entries a provenance gate calls unsupported in an agent's compaction summary are the agent's own earlier words, not inventions at summary time: at least half have an antecedent in the agent's prior assistant turns, and of those at least two in five were hedged when first written and are stated as fact in the summary, so what compaction lost is the hedge, not the source.
trick: Before calling a summary line unsourced, look in the one place the provenance judge never looks — the agent's own earlier messages — and check whether the line was a guess there that the summary rewrote as a fact.
why_now: Card 2611.06545 (2026-11) is the first corpus with a ground truth for 'unsupported' and a provenance trace into the writer's own text: 'In 46 of them the agent's earlier reasoning already paired an approval word with the restricted action, often as a guess ("Before publishing, I might need approval")' (sec. 5.6), '46 were own guesses (39 in the first turn; 28 of their earliest mentions were hedged), 17 appeared at the summary' (App. H), and 'All 46 development matches are in the agent's reasoning, none in its visible text, and for the 29 Qwen3 sources that reasoning was not in the writer's input at compaction' — its run records are released. SJC 2610.20927 (2026-10-14) shipped the delete-by-provenance gate whose source set excludes the assistant role, and its own limitation text says 'supported and unsupported entries are correct at similar rates (92.2% against 90.6%; Appendix G)' (quoted in the CL-W43-05 kill report), which is what one expects if the unsupported entries are the agent's own sensible plans rather than inventions. The CL-W43-05 kill (2026-11-01) left the 'entries nothing supports' cell as CL-W44-06's one-in-ten clause with no mechanism for where such entries come from; this is that mechanism.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 3 days): clone the handoff-audit release and Compact-Bench; run an SJC-style source judge (the paper's yes/no prompt, one frontier model, temperature 0) over every summary entry of 300 handoff-audit summaries (150 per model, stratified by template family) and of Compact-Bench's summaries for 35 repairs x 4 summarizers, to define $E_0$ on each corpus; verify the judge against the card paper's own rule labels on its policy sentences (agreement reported, not assumed). Step 1 ($0, 3 days): run the widening matcher at levels 1 to 3 with the shuffled-history placebo (entries matched against another task's history of the same template family), label hedges by a fixed marker list plus one reader pass on a 100-entry random sample (Cohen's kappa against the markers reported), and tabulate $u_1, u_2, u_3$ and $h$ per corpus, per summary section (facts, plans or TODOs, pending asks where the corpus has sections) and per writer, with template- or repair-clustered bootstrap intervals. Step 2 (about $250, 4 days): 50 AppWorld train+dev tasks x 1 run in the public SJC harness (OpenClaw safeguard compressor, 4,096-token window, GPT, temperature 0), SJC's own judge marks $E_0$ at every boundary, the matcher runs at levels 1 and 2 (no reasoning through the API) against the recorded transcript; same readouts. The headline quantifier is $u_1$ on each corpus and $h$ among the matched entries.
killing_experiment.kills_if: On two of the three corpora the clustered 95% lower bound of $u_1$ is above 0.75 (fewer than one in four gate-unsupported entries has any antecedent in the agent's own earlier visible turns) and $u_3$ on the open-weight corpora stays above 0.6 (reasoning does not close the gap either): the unsupported entries are born at summary time, SJC's noun ('no environment output supports') is right about origin as well as provenance, the summarization field's 'circumstantial inference' is the mechanism, and CL-W44-06's one-in-ten clause has no own-words mechanism and must stand on the failure census alone. A second kill for the hedge clause alone: $u_1 \leq 0.5$ but $h$'s upper bound below 0.2 (the agent's earlier statements were already unhedged, so compaction copied a confident claim and lost nothing), which leaves the source-set result standing as a definition note and kills the de-hedging mechanism. Protocol kill: the placebo chance-match rate within 5 points of the real level-1 match rate on any corpus voids that corpus's readout.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.55: $u_1 \leq 0.5$ on all three corpora (plans, TODOs and pending-ask entries nearly all have an assistant-turn antecedent; fact entries less often), $u_2$ a further 5 to 10 points lower where the system prompt names rules, $u_3 \leq 0.3$ on the gpt-oss corpus; among matched entries $h \in [0.4, 0.6]$, highest in the TODO and pending-ask sections and on the handoff-audit corpus whose own trace found 28 of 46 earliest mentions hedged; by writer, the Qwen3 writer, which does not see its reasoning at compaction, re-derives the same propositions with $h$ no lower than gpt-oss's, so the antecedent is the model's stable inference as much as a copied line.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: SJC 2610.20927: an unsupported entry is one 'no environment output supports' and the right action is to delete it (abstract; the +8.9 Pass3 recipe); its source set is environment outputs and the prior summary by definition. The summarization field: unsupported summary content is 'extrinsic hallucination' (Maynez et al. 2020, per the CL-W43-05 kill report) or 'Circumstantial Inference' generated at summary time (2406.03487, per the same report). The card paper itself traces own guesses for policy sentences only, on its own synthetic corpus, and says 'It does not show that this turn caused the summary sentence'. The single natural case in print, 2607.13071, reads one such entry as 'a conflation of observation and persistence' with no count.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If $u_1 \leq 0.5$ and $h \geq 0.4$: 'unsourced' is a property of the gate's source set, not of the writer's invention; the compactor's defect on these entries is modality loss (a guess restated as a fact), the provenance column must name its source set in every compaction census (C-W44-11's invented cell included), the recipe consequence is to carry the entry's epistemic status (guess, plan, confirmed) rather than delete it — transparent-compact 2610.20116, which keeps assistant prose verbatim, is the existing arm that preserves the hedge and its gain gets a mechanism — and CL-W44-06's 'not entries nothing supports' clause gains the mechanism it lacks. If $u_1 \geq 0.75$: the entries are born at the summary, SJC's deletion is aimed at the right object, and the pipeline's census cells are correct as drawn.

scorecard.target_value: In print: the card paper's closing question on where unsupported policy comes from and its own-guess trace (sec. 5.6, App. H); SJC's limitation that provenance and correctness 'are largely independent' (Appendix G, per the CL-W43-05 kill report) with no account of what the unsupported entries are; 2607.13071's case of observation conflated with persistence; OpenAI's monitors flagging self-written instructions in '2.15% and 0.27% of reinforcement-learning compaction summaries of two models' (card sec. 1), where a monitor judges 'unsupported' without the writer's reasoning. Who pays: compactor builders choosing between delete-by-provenance and carry-the-status; compaction evaluators defining the provenance axis; monitor builders deciding whether an unsupported instruction is an invention or a promoted guess.

impact_ceiling.floor: A three-corpus table of the unmatched share by source-set level and the de-hedged share, cited by the next compaction census and by CL-W44-06's write-up as the origin of its 'not entries nothing supports' clause. Requires steps 0 and 1. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: Compaction censuses report the provenance axis per source set (environment-only, plus assistant turns, plus system prompt) and the hedge-loss share as a standard column; one benchmark (Compact-Bench or HSC-Bench) adopts it; SJC's gate is re-read as deleting the agent's own plans. Requires steps 0 to 2 agreeing. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: Modality loss becomes the named mechanism of self-written-instruction failures: a status-carrying compaction format (guess / plan / confirmed per entry) is tested against delete-by-provenance at matched tokens on SJC's harness and the production-log monitors (OpenAI's 2.15% and 0.27%) are re-read for promoted guesses; the lane's provenance column is replaced by a status column. Requires the recipe arm (about $700 more on the SJC harness) and a second writer family. Judgment p 0.1.

scorecard.relevance: Narasimhan (self-evolving agents, memory): direct, the status of a memory entry is the axis his memory work lacks. HAL and evaluators: moderate, a column. Systems routes: zero. Industry (compaction and orchestrator teams, monitor builders): direct. Jacob's edge: computer engineering small (the matcher is text processing); theoretical physics zero.
scorecard.kill_probe: Steps 0 and 1 at $0 on the released handoff-audit records and Compact-Bench pairs, 6 days; step 2 at most $250 in the SJC harness, 4 days; 0 GPU-hours; dead if on two of three corpora the lower bound of $u_1$ is above 0.75 and $u_3$ above 0.6.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: Occupied by the card: the own-guess / rejection / at-summary trace for policy sentences on its synthetic corpus (46 / 1 / 17 of 64 development sources; 85 of 110 held-out followed a rejection) and the hedged-first-mention count (28 of 46); the card does not trace non-policy entries, does not run on a natural agent corpus, and does not compute an unmatched share against a provenance gate's set. SJC owns the gate and its source definition; transparent-compact 2610.20116 owns the verbatim-assistant-prose recipe (per the CL-W43-05 kill report); 2607.13071 owns the single case; 2406.03487 and 2005.00661 own the summarization taxonomies this would be an import of (intrinsic misuse of source content, here the agent's own prose, versus extrinsic invention). Within the pipeline: C-W44-11 counts failures by cell with the environment-and-summary source set and would over-count its invented cell if this is right; C-W44-13 counts unsourced entries by write regime with the same set; C-W43-09 (label instead of delete) died as a recipe variant and is the recipe this census would revive only if $h$ is high. The kill search must use the neighbours' role words (hedge, modal, epistemic marker, certainty, overclaiming, uncertainty preservation, faithfulness of attribution, intrinsic versus extrinsic hallucination, own-turn provenance, self-citation) and quote the limitation text of SJC (Appendix G) and transparent-compact; density counted on the day of writing.
scorecard.why_now: Card 2611.06545 (2026-11): released run records with reasoning, a ground-truth 'unsupported', and the own-guess trace with 28 of 46 hedged; SJC 2610.20927 (2026-10-14) public harness and judge; Compact-Bench 2610.31710 (2026-10-22) public pairs; the CL-W43-05 kill (2026-11-01) that left the invented cell without a mechanism. Nothing in the method is new (string matching and a marker list); the enabling piece is a corpus where 'unsupported' has a ground truth and the writer's reasoning is on disk.
scorecard.register_and_not: Measurement (a provenance census re-run with a widening source set and a hedge count on three corpora) with a definitional consequence (name the source set; report hedge loss) and a pointer to an existing recipe arm. It is not a new compaction recipe, not a judge of correctness, not a failure census (that is C-W44-11), and not a claim that the agent's own earlier words are true: SJC's 92.2% versus 90.6% says correctness is a separate axis.

identifiability: Random given: one corpus, one writer model at its recorded sampling settings (handoff-audit: Qwen3 at temperature 0.6, gpt-oss at 1.0; Compact-Bench: the summarizers' recorded settings; SJC harness: GPT at temperature 0), one source judge at temperature 0 (its decision variance is serving noise only, reported from a 50-entry re-judge), one matcher with fixed thresholds and a placebo rate. The unmatched share is a property of the (entry set, source set, matcher) triple and the headline names all three; the de-hedged share depends on the marker list and is checked by a reader on a 100-entry sample. On the Qwen3 corpus the reasoning antecedent was not in the writer's input, so a level-3 match there is evidence of a stable model inference, not of copying; the record reports level-3 matches split by whether the antecedent was in the writer's input. The judge's unsupported set $E_0$ is defined by the gate's own prompt, so the result is about what the gate marks, which is the object the recipe acts on.

title: Whose budget? The tight-turn collapse of multi-turn RL read with the prompt held fixed and one attempt instead of eight (v2: designed after the concept-level kill search of CL-W45-03, with GiGPO-Full as the in-print reference and the two one-quantifier claims 03a / 03b)
glossary: Turn cap $T$: the maximum number of agent actions an episode may use; $T_{\max} = 70$ on FrozenLake, so 25% of cap is $T_{25} = 17$ (the paper's rounding at 25% is not stated; BudgetMix uses $\lceil k T_{\max} / 10 \rceil$, so we pre-register $T_{25} = \lceil 0.25 \cdot 70 \rceil = 18$ and report 17 beside it). Announced prompt: the paper's protocol, the system prompt states the cap, the turns completed and the turns remaining before every action (Table 2). Held prompt: the prompt keeps stating $T_{\max}$ and the matching counters while the episode is cut silently at $T$; the first $T$ turns of a held rollout are distributed exactly as the first $T$ turns of a full-cap rollout, so the held reading at every $T$ is a count on the full-cap rollouts. $\mathrm{Pass}@(K,T)$: probability that at least one of $K$ independent episodes, each cut at $T$ turns, is a verified success; $K = 1$ is single-attempt success. Gap $g_K(T) = \mathrm{Pass}@(K,T)_{\mathrm{RL}} - \mathrm{Pass}@(K,T)_{\mathrm{base}}$. Collapse $C = g_8(T_{\max}) - g_8(T_{25})$ under the announced protocol (in print at Qwen3-4B GRPO-Full: $10.8 - (-1.6) = 12.4$ points). Retention $\rho = g_K(T_{25}) / g_K(T_{\max})$. Coverage term $\kappa = g_1(T_{25}) - g_8(T_{25})$ under the announced protocol: how much the gap moves when eight tries are replaced by one. Full-budget RL: trained only at $T_{\max}$ with the announced prompt. GiGPO: GRPO plus a step-level advantage from actions taken at recurring environment states across the group (one sentence: credit per step without a critic). Structural ceiling: the share of test maps whose shortest path fits in $T$ turns (App. B.3; the released toolkit computes it by BFS).
statement: Train one Full-budget GRPO agent at Qwen3-4B on FrozenLake with the paper's App. A recipe ($G = 16$, $T_{\max} = 70$, Table 2 prompt, lr $10^{-6}$, KL 0.001, training temperature 1.0) and, if that run finishes under 60 GPU-h, one Full-budget GiGPO agent at matched optimizer steps and rollouts. Roll out base, GRPO-Full (and GiGPO-Full) $n = 16$ times on each of $M = 1000$ generated held-out maps at the paper's evaluation temperature 0.6 and top-$p$ 0.9: (a) at $T_{\max}$ with the announced prompt, recording for every rollout the turn of termination and the evaluator's termination reason in {success, environment_terminal, budget_exhausted}; (b) at $T_{25}$ with the announced prompt (primary), and at 50% and 75% (secondary). The held reading at every $T$ is computed from (a) by the truncation identity $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)^{\mathrm{held}}(x) = p_T(x) = \Pr_{\tau \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x, T_{\max})}[R(\tau) = 1,\ \ell(\tau) \le T]$ ($x$ the map, $R \in \{0,1\}$ the verifier, $\ell(\tau)$ the turns used) and $\mathrm{Pass}@(K,T)^{\mathrm{held}}$ by the without-replacement estimator on the indicator $\{R = 1, \ell \le T\}$; one explicit cut-at-$T_{25}$ run with the toolkit's paired seeds on 200 maps is a serving-noise calibration of that identity, not a finding. Readouts, each with a 95% map-cluster bootstrap band and reported on all maps and on the stratum feasible at $T_{25}$: the four 25%-cap gaps (announced or held, $K = 8$ or $K = 1$), the full-cap $K = 1$ and $K = 8$ gaps, the retention $\rho$ under each reading, the coverage term $\kappa$, the collapse $C$, the turns-to-success distributions of each policy at full cap by shortest-path stratum, the three-way termination split at $T_{25}$ under both prompts, and the same table for GiGPO-Full beside the in-print reference rows.

CL-W45-03a.headline: On FrozenLake (Qwen3-4B, Full-budget GRPO, $T_{\max} = 70$), with the prompt's budget line held at $T_{\max}$ and the episode cut silently at 25% of the cap, the RL-minus-base $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ gap keeps at least half of its full-cap value: $g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25}) \ge \tfrac{1}{2}\, g_1(T_{\max})$.
CL-W45-03a.what_it_is: By the truncation identity this is a statement about the two policies' turns-to-success distributions at full cap: at least half of RL's extra single-attempt successes land within the first 18 turns. It is the prompt-free reading of the paper's conjecture ('agent RL primarily strengthens long-horizon capabilities whose benefits emerge when sufficient interaction budget is available', sec. 3.2). The prompt term proper is the announced-minus-held difference $\Delta_\pi(T) = g^{\mathrm{ann}} - g^{\mathrm{held}}$ at fixed $K$ (import S8xF9's P1) and is reported beside it.
CL-W45-03a.kills_if: Primary (absolute form): $g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25}) \le 0$ points with the 95% map-cluster band excluding $\tfrac{1}{2}\, g_1(T_{\max})$. Guard: if $g_1(T_{\max}) < 5$ points the ratio is not resolvable at this $n$ and 03a is recorded 'not resolvable', with the absolute gaps reported; the claim is then re-filed on the absolute gap or parked. Secondary: the retention $\hat\rho_1^{\mathrm{held}}$ and its band are reported but do not decide (simulated band half-width about 0.28 at $M = 1000$, see power). Negative outcome is informative: RL's extra successes are late-trajectory under a prompt-free reading, the paper's conjecture holds, and the fix belongs in training (BudgetMix or a turns-used term).
CL-W45-03a.expected: Judgment 0.25 that 03a holds (down from the v1 record's 0.55, after AdaTurn Table 1 and the paper's own 8B rows). Field assumes: budget dependence (sec. 3.2, App. B.3, AnySearch 2609.00813).

CL-W45-03b.headline: On FrozenLake (Qwen3-4B, Full-budget GRPO) under the paper's announced protocol at 25% of the cap, replacing eight tries by one moves the RL-minus-base gap by at least half of the announced-protocol collapse: $\kappa = g_1^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) - g_8^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) \ge \tfrac{1}{2}\, C$, with $C = g_8(T_{\max}) - g_8(T_{25})$ (in print 12.4 points at 4B, so the headline requires $g_1^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) \ge +4.6$ while $g_8^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) = -1.6$).
CL-W45-03b.what_it_is: The coverage term: $\mathrm{Pass}@8$ rewards spread across eight tries, and a flatter base model collects that bonus; if RL is sharper (per-map success concentrated), the single-attempt gap at a tight cap is larger than the eight-try gap.
CL-W45-03b.kills_if: $\hat\kappa \le \tfrac{1}{4}\, \hat C$ with the 95% band excluding $\tfrac{1}{2}\, \hat C$ (at the in-print $C$: $\hat\kappa \le 3.1$ points, band excluding 6.2). A negative $\hat\kappa$ (RL gains more from breadth than the base, the 2604.14877 Table 2 pattern) kills it outright and is reported as the lane's first multi-turn $K = 1$ versus $K = 8$ reading at a binding cap. Guard: both readings are repeated at temperature 1.0 (step 3) because $\kappa$ is a property of the sampling temperature.
CL-W45-03b.expected: Judgment 0.3 that 03b holds. In print: 2604.14877 Table 2 (silent cap, HotPotQA bridge, $T = 1$ of 5): $g_1 = -3.5$, $g_4 = 0.0$, $g_{16} = +1.7$, $g_{64} = +4.0$, so $\kappa < 0$ there at every $T$; Sharpening Tax 2610.01509 (single-turn agentic benchmarks, no cap): post-training raises pass@1 and lowers pass@K, so $\kappa > 0$ there. The paper's own Fig. 2 at full cap has RL above base at every $K$ to 128 with the gap growing in $K$ ('the RL model consistently outperforms the base model as the sampling breadth $k$ increases'), which is $\kappa(T_{\max}) < 0$; 03b therefore needs the sign of $\kappa$ to flip between $T_{\max}$ and $T_{25}$.

gate4_hypothesis.mechanism_sentence: The announced-protocol collapse of a Full-budget policy has two protocol terms that any policy evaluated this way carries (an unfamiliar counter value the policy never saw in training, and the eight-try coverage bonus of the flatter policy) plus one policy term (where in the trajectory its extra successes land); GRPO-Full crosses zero and GiGPO-Full / PPO-Full do not at 4B because GRPO's trajectory-level credit displaces the policy furthest from the base at the trajectory level (the paper's cumulative LLR about 228 vs 26 for successful trajectories, Terminal-Bench, sec. 4.1), which makes an unseen counter value most disruptive to it and its full-cap lead the smallest of the three (10.8 vs 14.9 and 18.4), while the step-level signals of GiGPO and PPO keep single-step behaviour closer to the base and so less sensitive to the counter.
gate4_hypothesis.pre_registered_prediction: (i) For GRPO-Full the held-prompt $K = 1$ drop $g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{\max}) - g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25})$ is smaller than the announced $K = 8$ drop $\hat C$ by at least half of $\hat C$. (ii) If the GiGPO arm runs: the part of the collapse removed by the held $K = 1$ reading is smaller for GiGPO-Full than for GRPO-Full (GiGPO's protocol terms are smaller), and GiGPO-Full's held $K = 1$ retention is at or above GRPO-Full's.
gate4_hypothesis.refuting_observation: GRPO-Full's held-prompt $K = 1$ drop is at least as large as its announced $K = 8$ drop minus the band (the protocol terms remove nothing; the collapse is where RL's successes land), or the GiGPO arm shows protocol terms as large as GRPO's with the same policy term (then the credit signal is not what separates the arms). The 8B rows already in print (GiGPO-Full retention 0.05) say the hypothesis's 'GiGPO does not collapse' clause is size-dependent; the probe is at 4B and tests the 4B form only, and the record says so.

Two of its assumptions are conservative for the design as written: (i) base and RL per-map success probabilities are drawn independently, whereas map difficulty (shortest-path length, hole layout) is shared, and (ii) the full-cap gap is drawn on fresh maps, whereas the held reading at $T_{25}$ is a count on the same full-cap rollouts. The defender's simulation (redteam/defender/power_defender.py; four Beta marginals pinned to the same Table 1 cells, Gaussian copula with base-RL correlation $\rho$ and within-policy $T_{25}$-$T_{\max}$ correlation 0.8, nested success events) gives SD of $g_1(T_{25})$ at $n = 16$: $\rho = 0$: 2.5 / 1.9 / 1.4 at $M$ = 300 / 500 / 1000 (matches the attackers); $\rho = 0.5$: 2.0 / 1.5 / 1.0; $\rho = 0.7$: 1.7 / 1.3 / 1.0; $n = 32$ changes nothing beyond 0.1 (between-map variance dominates, as the attackers say). What resolves the absolute-form kill ('$\hat g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25}) \le 0$ with the 95% band excluding $\tfrac{1}{2} g_1(T_{\max})$'): at $\hat g = 0$ the band's upper edge is $1.96 \cdot \mathrm{SD}$, so the kill can fire iff $g_1(T_{\max}) > 3.92 \cdot \mathrm{SD}$; at $M = 1000$, $n = 16$ that is $g_1(T_{\max}) > 5.5$ points ($\rho = 0$, conservative) or $> 4.2$ ($\rho = 0.5$); at $M = 500$ it is $> 7.5$ / $> 6.1$. Pre-registration therefore: $M = 1000$, $n = 16$, and the 03a guard raised from 5 to 6 points (objection 13 fixes where the guard is measured). The confirm side is symmetric (claim holds if $\hat g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25}) \ge \tfrac{1}{2}\hat g_1(T_{\max})$ with the band excluding 0; resolvable under the same condition). Cost: $M = 1000 \times n = 16$ is 16,000 rollouts per (policy, cell); the primary grid is two cells per policy (full cap announced, which yields the held curve at every $T$ by the identity, and announced $T_{25}$), 64,000 rollouts, about 25-30 GPU-h under the paper's prompt form with thinking off (arithmetic in the answer to objection 9), so the whole solo probe is about 80-85 GPU-h, under one GPU-week. BudgetMix trains on every counter value, so its prompt term is zero by construction, and it is read at $K = 8$ like every other row, so its collapse $C_{\mathrm{BM}}$ is coverage term plus residual budget dependence. The record must carry these rows (conceded: it did not). The inference is accepted for the prompt term and rejected for the coverage term. Write the announced $K = 8$ collapse exactly as three terms (all prompts at $T_{\max}$ are the same under both regimes, so $g^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{\max}) = g^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{\max})$): $$C = \underbrace{g_1(T_{\max}) - g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25})}_{C_1^{\mathrm{held}}\ \text{(policy term)}} \;-\; \underbrace{\bigl[g_1^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) - g_1^{\mathrm{held}}(T_{25})\bigr]}_{D\ \text{(prompt term, gap level)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\bigl[\kappa(T_{25}) - \kappa(T_{\max})\bigr]}_{\text{coverage term}},$$ with $\kappa(T) = g_1^{\mathrm{ann}}(T) - g_8^{\mathrm{ann}}(T)$. For BudgetMix every counter value is in-distribution, so its $D_{\mathrm{BM}}$ is not zero but an adaptation gain (the announced tight counter helps a policy trained on it), which makes $C_{\mathrm{BM}}$ an under-statement of BudgetMix's silent-cap budget dependence; under the attackers' monotonicity assumption (budget-sampled training does not increase the policy term) this tightens, not loosens, the bound on GRPO-Full's prompt term: $-D_{\mathrm{Full}} \le C_{\mathrm{Full}} - C_{\mathrm{BM}} + (\text{coverage}_{\mathrm{BM}} - \text{coverage}_{\mathrm{Full}}) = 7.8$ (4B) / 7.3 (8B) points if GRPO-Full's coverage term is at least BudgetMix's. Accepted and written into the record as the in-print ceiling on the prompt term: at most 63% of the collapse at 4B and 34% at 8B. The step from there to 'the coverage term of GRPO-Full is at most 4.6' does not follow: it requires $\text{coverage}_{\mathrm{Full}} \le \text{coverage}_{\mathrm{BM}} + \text{policy}_{\mathrm{BM}}$, which assumes the thing 03b asserts is false (that GRPO-Full's per-map success is more concentrated than BudgetMix's). $\kappa > 0$ iff the base's eight-try spread $p_8 - p_1$ exceeds RL's; 03b at 4B needs $g_1^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) \ge +4.6$ with $g_8^{\mathrm{ann}}(T_{25}) = -1.6$, i.e. RL's $p_8 / p_1$ at $T_{25}$ about 1.5 against the base's about 2.2 under the assumed $\mathrm{Pass}@1$ values; no FrozenLake cell in print excludes it (the paper reports no $K = 1$ number at any cap; App. E.1 and E.3 show BudgetMix improves single-step quality relative to standard RL, a different policy from GRPO-Full). objections.objection: 03b's sign has zero multi-turn data points for it and two against. objections.answer: Partly answered, partly conceded; the judgment for 03b is lowered from 0.3 to 0.2. (i) The 2604.14877 data points are real and verified (Table 2, lines 547-785 of the fetched text): Category C, $T = 1$: base 0.307 / 0.492 / 0.609 / 0.670, RL 0.272 / 0.492 / 0.626 / 0.710; $T = 5$: base 0.363 / 0.535 / 0.675 / 0.770, RL 0.335 / 0.541 / 0.690 / 0.810; Category B shows the same sign ($T = 1$: $g_1 = +1.2$, $g_4 = +4.4$; $T = 5$: $g_1 = +9.2$, $g_4 = +16.9$). So $\kappa < 0$ at every depth and both categories there. But that paper also measured why: its RL policy is more diverse than its base, not sharper ('$\pi_{\mathrm{base}}$ produces a mean of 40.1 unique sequences per problem ... $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$ produces 45.5', line 237), so $\kappa < 0$ is the expected sign for a non-sharpening RL policy and the datum does not transfer to a policy that sharpens; whether 4B GRPO on FrozenLake sharpens is the open quantity, and the only sharpening evidence in the card paper (LLR 228 vs 26) is on Terminal-Bench, as the objection says. (ii) The second datum against is withdrawn by the defender as unsupported: the v2 record's own gloss 'with the gap growing in $K$' is not in the paper's text; sec. 3.1 and App. C say only that 'RL-trained models consistently outperform their base models as the number of sampled trajectories $K$ increases', which is RL above base at every $K$, and the sign of $\kappa(T_{\max})$ on FrozenLake cannot be read from Figure 2 without the plotted numbers. The record will say so. (iii) A mechanism for the sign changing between $T_{\max}$ and $T_{25}$ exists and is written: $\kappa(T) > 0$ iff the base's eight-try spread $p_8(T) - p_1(T)$ exceeds RL's; a policy's spread is largest on maps where its per-map success is intermediate and vanishes on maps where it is near 0 or 1; as $T$ tightens, maps that a late-succeeding policy solves at full cap move to $p \approx 0$ (spread lost) while a short-random-walk policy keeps intermediate $p$ on short maps (spread kept). So if RL's extra successes are late (the paper's conjecture, and 03a's failure mode), RL's spread shrinks faster than the base's as $T$ falls and $\kappa$ rises toward positive at $T_{25}$ even if it is negative at $T_{\max}$. That mechanism predicts 03b at the expense of 03a, which the record's pre-registered outcome table already names ('03a dies and 03b holds: the collapse is real at $K = 1$ but exaggerated by the coverage metric'). (iv) Conceded: with zero FrozenLake data points and the only same-sign datum single-turn (Sharpening Tax, abstract-level), 03b's pre-registered surprise rests on a mechanism and not on a published pattern; judgment 0.2. Its negative outcome remains the lane's first multi-turn $K = 1$ versus $K = 8$ reading at a binding cap and is reported either way.

Conceded: 03a is the policy term under a prompt-free reading (by the identity it is a statement about where RL's extra single-attempt successes land), not 'the prompt term'; the kill report's label was a misnomer and the record will say so. The parent headline has two parts and the probe now tests both. The released evaluator instead keeps the system prompt fixed and appends the counter to each observation message (prefix-friendly). The two are different protocols for the policy as well (where the counter sits in context) and differ by up to an order of magnitude in prefill tokens; the v2's 25 GPU-h for 128,000 rollouts is defensible only under the appended form with thinking off. Prefill under the paper's form is a prefix-cache miss every turn: with context at turn $t$ about $400 + 150t$ tokens (system + task + map, then action + observation per turn), a rollout of $L$ turns prefills $\sum_{t < L}(400 + 150t)$ tokens: 103k tokens at $L = 35$ (the assumed mean full-cap length), 19k at $L = 14$ (mean at $T_{25}$). objections.objection: The 'half of the full-cap lead' quantifier is bounded by a structural ceiling nobody has computed for these maps. If RL's lead is concentrated on long-path maps, 03a is dead by geometry (and that is budget dependence in the truest sense), independent of any prompt. The record must pre-register the feasible stratum as the primary population for 03a, report RL's full-cap lead by shortest-path stratum, and state the ceiling at $T_{25}$ before a GPU is used (the toolkit computes it: 'FrozenLake uses exact deterministic BFS ... structural ceilings'). The v2 has the gate (fewer than 500 feasible maps triggers regeneration) but regenerating maps to a chosen ceiling changes the benchmark the headline is about.

title: Graded by the wrong continuation: multi-turn RL's step quality under the base policy's own value on the states the trained policy visits
statement: On the FrozenLake GRPO checkpoint of the sibling probe (Qwen3-4B, App. A recipe), draw 200 histories from the RL policy's own full-cap trajectories in proportion to visitation and 200 from the base's, sample $G = 16$ actions from each policy at every history as the paper does, and score each action two ways: the paper's $Q^{*}(h, a)$ (dynamic programming under optimal continuation within the remaining budget, $\gamma = 0.95$) and $Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}(h, a)$, the success probability of taking $a$ at history $h$ and following the base policy afterwards, estimated by 4 Monte Carlo continuations at the paper's evaluation temperature. Readouts: the share of ordinary (non-error) histories on which the RL policy's mean action value exceeds the base's, by ruler ($Q^{*}$, $Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}$) and by state pool (symmetric as in App. B.4, RL-visited, base-visited); the mean base-relative advantage $\bar{A}^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}_t$ at each depth $t$ on RL-visited histories; and the identity check that $\sum_t \bar{A}^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}_t$ over RL trajectories equals the measured $\mathrm{Pass}@1$ gain within 3 points, with the share of that sum carried by the top 10% of steps and by post-error histories.
claim: On FrozenLake the sub-50% step-quality verdict on multi-turn RL is a ruler choice: judged by the base policy's own continuation on the histories the RL policy actually visits, the RL action is the better one on more than 60% of ordinary states.
trick: Grade each move by what the untrained agent would have made of it from there, and count the moves the trained agent actually makes; a half-and-half pool graded by a perfect player measures the perfect player's map, not the difference between the two agents.
why_now: The paper (2026-11-04) makes matched-state step grading the reading of what RL learned — 'To isolate action quality from state visitation bias, we construct a state evaluation pool by sampling intermediate states equally from base and RL trajectories' (sec. 3.3) — and grades against 'the exact $Q^{*}$ value of each step-level action under optimal continuation within the remaining interaction budget' (sec. 3.3); its training-dynamics ruler $R_{\mathrm{single}}$ fixes a pool of 512 base-model states (App. E.3). Continuation grading of agent steps is spreading (Probe-and-Resume 2610.21088, GiGPO anchor states 2505.10978), and none of it names the continuation policy or the state weights. The identity that fixes both is twenty-four years old (Kakade and Langford, conservative policy iteration, 2002) and absent from every one of these papers.

killing_experiment.design: Import, in plain words: the performance difference lemma says the total gain of a new policy over an old one is the sum, over the states the new policy actually visits, of how much better its moves are when judged by the old policy's own expected outcome from there. Written for a finite horizon, discount 1, deterministic environment: $$J(\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}) - J(\pi_{\mathrm{B}}) = \sum_{t=1}^{T_{\max}} \mathbb{E}_{h_t \sim d_t^{\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}},\ a_t \sim \pi_{\mathrm{RL}}(\cdot \mid h_t)} \bigl[ Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}(h_t, a_t) - V^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}(h_t) \bigr],$$ where $J(\pi)$ is the success probability ($\mathrm{Pass}@1$) of policy $\pi$, $d_t^{\pi}$ the distribution of histories at turn $t$ under $\pi$, $Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}(h, a)$ the success probability of taking $a$ at $h$ and following the base thereafter, and $V^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}(h) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\mathrm{B}}(\cdot \mid h)} Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}(h, a)$. The paper's ruler replaces $Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}$ by $Q^{*}$ and $d^{\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}}$ by a half-and-half pool. Step 1 (shared with the sibling probe, 0 marginal GPU-h): the Qwen3-4B GRPO FrozenLake checkpoint and $n = 16$ full-cap rollouts per held-out map for both policies. Step 2 (about 25 GPU-h, 3 days): 200 RL-visited and 200 base-visited ordinary histories (post-error histories tagged by the paper's App. B.5 construction kept as a separate stratum), 16 sampled actions per policy per history, exact $Q^{*}$ by DP, $Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}$ by 4 base continuations per (history, action) — about 50k short continuations; compute win shares with bootstrap bands over histories, the depth-wise $\bar{A}^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}_t$ on RL trajectories and the identity check against the measured $\mathrm{Pass}@1$ gain. Step 3 (optional, about 10 GPU-h): the same on DeepCoder-MT with unit-test continuation if its checkpoint exists.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Under $Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{B}}}$ on RL-visited ordinary histories the RL win share stays below 52% (bootstrap band over 200 histories), while the identity check passes (the summed advantage is within 3 points of the measured $\mathrm{Pass}@1$ gain) and more than 70% of that sum sits on post-error histories: the paper's reading — recovery, not step quality — survives the correct ruler, the claim is dead, and the residue is the identity check as a method note the next step-grading paper cites. Cost standalone (without the sibling's checkpoint): about 130 GPU-h.

title: The 50x on a clock: self-GRPO distillation against GRPO in node-hours, where rollouts inside a batch are nearly free and optimizer steps are not
statement: Re-run the paper's headline pair on one 8-GPU node with verl 0.8's native OPD and the paper's Table 2 recipe (Qwen3-4B-Base, DAPO-Math-17K, batch 64 prompts, response cap 7,168, lr $2 \times 10^{-6}$, KL off): GRPO at $G = 8$ to its 33.9% OOD macro mean@16, then OPD from that checkpoint at $G = 1$ (batch 64, the 50x setting) and at $G = 8$ (the 6x setting), each until it recovers 33.9% and for 20% more steps, with per-step wall-clock split into generation, teacher forward, log-probability recompute and update, and peak memory logged. Readouts: node-hours to 33.9% for the three arms, the ratios $\rho_{G=1}$ and $\rho_{G=8}$ (GRPO node-hours over OPD node-hours) beside the paper's FLOP ratios 50 and 6, and the per-step generation time as a function of rollouts per step, which is the mechanism.
claim: On one node, self-GRPO distillation's 50x FLOP saving over GRPO is under 8x in node-hours, because the $G = 1$ setting buys its FLOPs with eight times the optimizer steps on a decode-bound machine where a batch of 64 and a batch of 512 take nearly the same time to generate.
trick: Time the two runs on the same machine instead of counting multiplications: decoding a batch costs about the same whether it holds 64 or 512 sequences, so the setting that saves FLOPs by shrinking the batch and taking eight times the steps pays back in hours what it saved in FLOPs.
why_now: The paper (2611.08453, v1 2026-11-05) stakes the comparison on FLOPs — 'Wall-clock and GPU-hours entangle the training objective with implementation and hardware; FLOPs is the only implementation-invariant compute metric' (App. A) — reports no wall-clock, GPU-hours or memory for any pair, and says of its own headline setting that it 'takes longer in wall-clock time because it runs more optimizer steps' (App. I) while asking the field to 'report training FLOPs as an implementation-invariant measure' (Limitations). It names the counter-evidence it does not resolve: 'Lee et al. (2026) find OPD slower than GRPO in wall-clock time' (sec. 2), and the Thinking Machines blog's '7-10x fewer gradient steps $\Rightarrow$ 50-100x compute efficiency' claim 'reports no method-separated GPU-hours or wall clock' (bibliography note). verl 0.8 ships native OPD and all models and data are public, so the pair is a recipe file away.

killing_experiment.design: Mechanism, written first: on one node a batch of $B$ sequences decodes in about $L_{\max} \cdot t_{\mathrm{step}}(B)$ seconds, with $L_{\max}$ the longest response in the batch and $t_{\mathrm{step}}(B)$ the per-token latency of one decode step, nearly flat in $B$ until the KV-cache memory limit; the FLOP ledger charges $10 N_s$ per generated token, linear in $B$. The $G = 1$ run has $B = 64$, the $G = 8$ runs $B = 512$, so per optimizer step they take nearly the same generation time while $G = 1$ needs 8x the steps per rollout. Step 0 (2 GPU-h, 1 day): measure $t_{\mathrm{step}}(B)$ for $B \in \{64, 128, 256, 512\}$ at 4B with SGLang on the node; if $t_{\mathrm{step}}(512) / t_{\mathrm{step}}(64) > 4$ the mechanism is absent on this node and the probe stops (informative: the node is compute-bound and the FLOP ledger is right there). Step 1 (about 80 GPU-h, 2 days): GRPO per Tables 2-3 to 200 steps, evaluating mean@16 on AIME24, AIME25, AMC23 (143 prompts) every 20 steps; record node-hours at the first crossing of 33.9 minus 1 and plus 1. Step 2 (about 40 GPU-h, 2 days): OPD from the step-200 GRPO checkpoint at $G = 1$ and at $G = 8$ with Table 4 settings (top-16 closed-form reverse KL, teacher temperature 1.0), same evaluation cadence, run to recovery plus 20%; per-step timing split and peak memory logged for every arm; the teacher is resident on the same node as in the paper (App. B.4: 'a single 8-GPU H200 node'). Step 3 (0 GPU-h): the table of node-hours vs FLOPs for the three arms and the fitted $t_{\mathrm{step}}(B)$ curve, so another node's ratio can be predicted from its own curve.
killing_experiment.kills_if: GRPO's node-hours to the 33.9% band exceed 25 times OPD-$G=1$'s on the same node (ratio at or above 25, with step 0 showing $t_{\mathrm{step}}$ flat in $B$ so the mechanism was present and still did not bite): the FLOP ledger's magnitude survives the clock within a factor of two, the claim is dead, and the residue is the first node-hour table for the pair, which the paper asks the field for and does not give.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.6: $\rho_{G=1}$ between 2 and 8, $\rho_{G=8}$ between 4 and 12, and the $G = 8$ distillation run reaches 33.9% in fewer node-hours than the $G = 1$ run despite eight times its FLOPs; generation is above 70% of per-step time in every arm, the teacher forward under 10%.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: The paper: 'FLOPs is the only implementation-invariant compute metric' and the 50x headline; the Thinking Machines blog's 50-100x; the three audited papers that report wall-clock wins do so at mismatched group sizes. The field reads the 50x as a cost ratio a consumer would see.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If under 8x: every FLOP-based efficiency claim for an RL or OPD recipe must state the batch shape and give node-hours beside it; the $G = 1$ recipe is retired for single-node users; L3 gets a datum that RL training cost on a node is sequential decode steps, not FLOPs. If at or above 25x: the FLOP ledger is vindicated as a cost proxy for this pair and the lane stops asking for wall-clock here.

Who pays: every team choosing between GRPO and distillation from its own checkpoints on a fixed node budget, and the multi-domain 'specialize, then consolidate' recipe whose 42% saving is also a FLOP number.

Requires two more nodes and three more recipes. Judgment p 0.1.

title: Same interactions, not same money: the hidden frontier judge in a self-distillation step-credit recipe, and GRPO given the same budget as rollouts
statement: Step 0, no GPU: from ORSD's released launchers and its App. C, count per training step the frozen-verifier calls (8 tasks x 4 rubric bundles x 8 trajectories = 256 calls to Qwen3.5-Plus through the DashScope API, each reading a group's transcripts with a 1,536-token output cap), the 32 rubric generations (4,096-token cap, policy at temperature 0.3) and the two privileged-replay log-probability passes, price them with the card's ledger ($10 N_s$ per student generated token, $2 N$ per frozen forward, API calls at the vendor's list price on the day) over the paper's 300 steps, and set the total beside the GRPO baseline's cost from its own launcher; do the same from the text for BLPO (rule-based progress summaries, Table 3 overhead) and AttnSR (one attention replay forward) as the two cheap controls. Step 1: on ALFWorld with Qwen3-1.7B using ORSD's own `run_alfworld_matched_grpo_4gpu_b8_n8_s300.sh`, run GRPO at $G = 8$ (calibration against the reported 53.92) and at $G = 16$ (twice the rollouts, a lower bound of the overhead measured in step 0), 300 steps, the paper's held-out protocol; compare with the reported ORSD 66.04. Readouts: the cost ratio of ORSD to its baseline in FLOPs and in dollars, the same for BLPO and AttnSR, and the share of the 12.1-point gap closed by rollout-matched GRPO.
claim: The 12-point ALFWorld gain ORSD reports over GRPO at 1.7B 'under the same environment-interaction budget' is a budget artefact: GRPO given the recipe's hidden verifier and replay spend as extra rollouts closes more than half of it.
trick: Price the judge: the recipe calls a frontier model on every trajectory for every candidate rubric at every step, so spend that money on more rollouts for the plain baseline and see whether the gap survives.
why_now: Three critic-free step-credit recipes on ALFWorld and WebShop landed in one week, each claiming a matched budget in a different unit: BLPO 'under matched training budgets' with 'little computational overhead' (2611.03005, 2026-11-02), ORSD 'under the same environment-interaction budget' and 'without introducing additional environment interactions' (2611.06543, 2026-11-04), AttnSR 'without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts' (2611.07932, 2026-11-05). ORSD's App. C states 'Frozen verifier Qwen3.5-Plus via DashScope API' and 'Verifier calls, replay computation, and wall-clock time are recorded separately' and reports none of them. 2611.08453 supplies the discipline — 'Fewer rollouts or optimizer steps therefore need not mean fewer FLOPs' — and the ledger. The released GRPO launcher makes the rollout-matched baseline a one-flag change.

killing_experiment.design: Import, in plain words: a controlled comparison matches the resource the consumer pays for (dollars or node-hours), and a recipe's claimed saving in another unit is converted before it is compared; this is the FLOP-ledger discipline of 2611.08453 carried from OPD to step credit. Step 0 ($0, 2 days): the ledger from code and text for the three recipes — ORSD: 76,800 verifier calls per run (256 per step x 300) with their input transcripts, 9,600 rubric generations, two replay log-probability passes over every rollout token (charged $2 N_s$ each); BLPO: rule-based summaries, Table 3 advantage-computation time; AttnSR: one replay forward with attention output ($2 N_s$ per token); each as a multiple of its own GRPO or PPO baseline's generated-token FLOPs and, for the API, in dollars at list price. If ORSD's multiple is under 1.5x in both units, stop: the claim is dead at step 0 and the ledger is the residue. Step 1 (about 140 GPU-h on four A100 80GB, 8 days): ORSD's own GRPO launcher at $G = 8$ (calibration; the run is accepted if its step-300 overall success is within 3 points of 53.92) and at $G = 16$ with everything else fixed (8 tasks per update, 300 steps, lr $10^{-6}$, the paper's held-out evaluation every 50 steps); read the step-300 overall success and the whole curve against the paper's Figure 3. Step 2 (optional, about 100 GPU-h): $G = 24$ if step 0 puts ORSD's multiple above 3x; and ORSD rerun with the policy itself as verifier (zero API) to separate judge distillation from rubric structure.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Our GRPO $G = 8$ reproduces 53.9 within 3 points and GRPO $G = 16$ lands below 60.0 at step 300 (closing under half of the 12.1-point gap to 66.04); or step 0 finds ORSD's verifier plus replay cost under 1.5x its baseline in both FLOPs and dollars: the gain is not an accounting artefact, the claim is dead, and the residue is the published ledger of the three recipes' hidden costs, which the W44 definitive-comparison spec (C-W44-DEF-L2) needs anyway.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5: step 0 puts ORSD's extra spend above 3x its baseline in dollars (the API verifier reads every transcript four times per step) and above 1.5x in student FLOPs (two replay passes plus rubric generation); GRPO at $G = 16$ reaches at least 60 at 1.7B, closing at least half of the gap; BLPO and AttnSR come in under 1.2x, so the ledger exonerates two of the three and the headline is about the unit, not about step credit.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: ORSD: the gain comes from 'extracting additional supervision from existing trajectories' (sec. 4.2) at 'the same environment-interaction budget'; the parked W44 spec matched sampled tokens; the lane's recipe papers match interactions, rollouts or steps and treat an LLM judge as free. GiGPO (a free step-credit recipe) does not beat GRPO in ORSD's own Table 1 (53.00 vs 53.92 at 1.7B), which the paper does not discuss.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If the gap closes: 'matched budget' claims in agent RL must state the unit and price judge calls; a process signal scored by a frontier API model is judge distillation, not self-distillation; GRPO at a larger group is the mandatory baseline for any recipe with an LLM in the loop. If it does not: the rubric signal is worth its price on ALFWorld at 1.7B, and the next question is the self-verifier arm.
